Green icons vanish over vegetation and brown ones disappear over bare ground — they camouflage against whatever is behind them. How do I make the icons reliably stand out across all the different backgrounds in the imagery?,"Below is a **step‑by‑step recipe** that turns “green disappears in the forest / brown disappears on the field” into **icons that stay readable on any satellite or aerial image**.
All of the recommendations come from the *maplibre‑cartography* skill – they work for MapLibre GL JS 1.x and 2.x and are safe for both desktop and mobile browsers.

column3: The icon’s hue is the same hue that the photo already contains. MapLibre can’t add a “background” behind the icon – it only paints the pixels you give it.
The photo supplies the only contrast, so wherever the photo is green/ brown the icon blends in.
A flat icon looks like a sticker that can float above the photo, which makes it even harder to separate.

column1: The fix is **to give the icon its own contrast layer** (a halo/outline or a shadow) **and to keep the icon’s fill highly saturated** so the chroma axis (color intensity) is different from the low‑saturation background of most imagery.
## 2. Use **SDF** (Signed‑Distance‑Field) sprites – the only way to add a halo in the style
### 2.1. Convert your SVG/PNG icons to SDF
# Put all SVGs you want to use in ./icons/
* The SVG must be **monochrome** (single fill colour, e.g. `#ffffff`).
* Keep a generous `viewBox` padding (≥ 10 % of the width/height) – the halo will be drawn outside the original shape, and you don’t want it clipped.
* If you need a gradient or a 3‑D look, bake it **into the SVG** (e.g. a linear gradient that goes from light‑top to dark‑bottom). The gradient stays when the image is rasterised for the SDF.
### 2.2. Load the sprite in the style
> **Never point a production style at `raw.githubusercontent.com`** – it is rate‑limited and may return 404 for anonymous users (see the skill references).
""icon-image"": ""my‑icon"",          // matches the ID in the sprite JSON
// 1️⃣ Saturated fill – choose a hue that is *not* common in imagery.
// 2️⃣ Dark, semi‑transparent halo that works on bright *and* dark ground.
// 3️⃣ Optional: a thin lighter inner halo for extra contrast on very dark ground.
//    (use only if the dark halo looks too heavy on bright fields)

## 4. Add a **contact shadow** (ground‑anchor) – optional but makes the icon feel “placed”
A contact shadow is a blurred ellipse that sits **under** the icon, not a drop‑shadow that lifts it.
*Place this layer **below** the symbol layer* (add it first in the `layers` array). The ellipse will stretch with the map pitch, giving the impression that the icon sits on the terrain.

## 6. When you *must* use a raster PNG (no SDF)
If you cannot rebuild the sprite as SDF, bake the outline/halo **into the PNG itself**:
1. In your graphics editor, add a **2 px stroke** around the shape.
3. Add a **soft drop‑shadow** that is offset **down‑and‑right** by ~1 px and blurred (radius ≈ 2 px).
4. Export with a transparent background and a generous canvas margin (so the halo isn’t clipped).
> **Caveat:** The halo will be *fixed* – you cannot change its colour or width at runtime. If you ever need a different colour scheme, you’ll have to re‑export the PNG.

column1: anti-pattern — reducing road opacity to calm bright roads on imagery,skills/maplibre-cartography/SKILL.md,I dropped my OSM Bright vector road layers on top of satellite imagery and the bright orange/yellow roads look garish and dominate the map. My instinct is to lower their opacity so the imagery shows through. Is that the right fix?,"### Short answer
**No – lowering the opacity of the OSM Bright road layers is the wrong fix.**

A semi‑transparent orange/yellow line lets the busy photographic background bleed through, which makes the road network look “washed‑out” and destroys the visual hierarchy you need when the basemap is imagery.

Instead, **re‑tone the road palette, keep the lines opaque, and let width & casing do the hierarchy work**. The steps below follow the cartographic best‑practice checklist from the **maplibre‑cartography** skill.

column3: The bright hue already competes with the unpredictable colors of satellite imagery. Adding transparency lets the underlying colors show through, so the road line can look brown on a field, green on a forest, or pink on a roof – all of which look like “stains” rather than a reference layer.

Road importance is normally encoded by width and casing contrast. When you make the line translucent the casing (often a darker line underneath) becomes hard to see, so a minor road can look as heavy as a highway.

WCAG contrast is calculated on the *combined* foreground+background. A 0.6‑opacity orange over a bright field may drop below the 4.5:1 ratio required for normal text‑size labels that sit on the same road line.
Transparent fragments force the GPU to blend each pixel, which is a tiny but unnecessary cost when you could simply draw an opaque, well‑contrasted line.
